implementation_notes: The sequential arrow-core realization: each independent check is a block inside either { zipOrAccumulate(...) { a, b, c -> ... } }, and failures accumulate into NonEmptyList<E>. Choose it when the checks are cheap and deterministic order of messages matters; the trade-off is that nothing runs concurrently.
pitfalls: Accumulation is lost as soon as one check is written with bind instead of a block.
Error order is argument order here - moving a check changes the message order users see.

variants.name: Arrow zipOrAccumulate (sequential accumulation)
variants.implementation_notes: The sequential arrow-core realization: each independent check is a block inside either { zipOrAccumulate(...) { a, b, c -> ... } }, and failures accumulate into NonEmptyList<E>. Choose it when the checks are cheap and deterministic order of messages matters; the trade-off is that nothing runs concurrently.
pitfalls: Accumulation is lost as soon as one check is written with bind instead of a block.
Error order is argument order here - moving a check changes the message order users see.

variants.name: parZipOrAccumulate / parMapOrAccumulate (concurrent accumulation)
variants.implementation_notes: The concurrent arrow-core realization: parZipOrAccumulate (and parMapOrAccumulate over collections) runs the independent checks concurrently and still accumulates every failure into NonEmptyList. Choose it when checks involve IO or heavy computation; the trade-off is completion-order error lists and the need for coroutine-aware cancellation handling.
pitfalls: Error order follows completion order, not source order: never rely on the first element of the accumulated list.
Concurrent blocks share the coroutine scope: an exception in one block cancels siblings, so real failures and cancellation must be distinguished.
